content.text: {"grade":4,"complete":false,"main_gap":"Claim 3.2 assumes without proof that every minimal transversal of C is finite; the final peeling argument critically needs this for a transversal obtained inside an infinite set.","errors":[{"description":"A minimal transversal of a family of finite, pairwise-intersecting sets need not be finite. Thus π(T) may be undefined, and the argument proves self-duality only for finite minimal transversals. For example, the family {{x,t_n}:n≥1} has the infinite minimal transversal {t_n:n≥1}.","quote":"Let $T$ be a minimal (under inclusion) transversal of $\\mathcal C$... Hence $\\pi(T)\\in S_\\infty$"},{"description":"At the decisive final application of Zorn, the contained minimal transversal may be infinite. Its finiteness is obtained only by invoking the unproved full self-duality, so the combinatorial theorem cannot validly be applied to the constructed family.","quote":"by (a) it contains a minimal transversal $T$, and $T\\in\\mathcal C$ by (iii). Since $T$ is finite"},{"description":"The Zorn ordering is stated inconsistently: under reverse inclusion, an intersection is an upper bound, and Zorn yields a maximal element in that order, not a minimal one. This is repairable by correcting the order terminology.","quote":"Consider transversals contained in $W$ ordered by reverse inclusion... So chains have lower bounds; by Zorn's lemma there is a minimal transversal"}],"notes":"Steps 1–2 and the intersecting property are sound. The proof’s central finiteness reduction is promising, but the infinite-minimal-transversal issue is substantive rather than a routine omitted detail."}
